strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: demographic bias in medical-image diagnosis. The distinction between clinically mediated demographic effects and potentially spurious image-based effects is a worthwhile motivation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/294b34078c0740f7a5999bb6f13b22f7/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation covers three public medical datasets, reports predictive and fairness metrics, and compares against vanilla training, adversarial debiasing, and FAAP. The reported results consistently improve DP, EO, and ADF, with relatively modest AUC reductions.

The parameter sweeps over perturbation strength and loss weights expose the expected fairness-utility trade-off, while experiments with ResNet18, ResNet50, and ViT provide some evidence that the masking approach is not tied to one architecture.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly, and the causal graph, framework diagram, tables, and qualitative GradCAM examples make the intended method accessible.
weaknesses: The central causal argument is technically unsound. Equation 1 defines a total causal effect using observational conditional probabilities rather than interventional distributions. The path-specific effects are asserted without stating the structural equations, cross-world counterfactuals, identification assumptions, or adjustment conditions required to identify them from the available observational data.

The proof of Theorem 1 contains consequential algebraic errors. In moving to Equation 14, the factor P(X|Y) introduced by Bayes' rule is dropped, and the derivation does not properly marginalize over X. Thus the claimed implication from I(S;X|Y)=0 to the proposed direct-effect criterion is not established by the presented proof.

The discussion immediately following Theorem 2 reverses the theorem's implication: the theorem states that I(S;X|Y)=0 is sufficient for I(S;Y-hat|Y)=0, but the text claims that I(S;Y-hat|Y)=0 is sufficient for I(S;X|Y)=0. Consequently, a small ADF cannot certify the training objective or the proposed path-specific Diagnosis Fairness. This breaks the main justification for the new evaluation metric.

ADF, defined as I(S;Y-hat|Y), is a standard conditional-independence or separation condition closely related to equalized odds, rather than clearly a novel causal metric. The paper does not adequately distinguish it from existing conditional fairness definitions. Moreover, conditioning on the observed diagnosis does not by itself show that a particular causal path has been removed.

The implemented adversarial loss only makes a particular discriminator less able to infer S. It does not demonstrate that the true conditional mutual information is minimized; a weak or unconverged discriminator can produce the same observation. The manuscript omits the discriminator and generator architectures, optimization schedule, MI estimation details for the training losses and ADF, and adversarial convergence diagnostics.

The empirical protocol is insufficient for the clinical and robustness claims. It reports one 90/10 split without clarifying whether splitting is patient-level, provides no validation protocol, cohort sizes after filtering, class and gender distributions, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Hyperparameters appear to be selected using the same reported results, creating a risk of test-set tuning.

The baseline set is narrow, and there are no comparisons with stronger contemporary fairness approaches or a direct equalized-odds objective. The downstream-task experiment lacks corresponding vanilla and component-controlled results, so it does not establish that the mutual-information pretraining improves data utility. The architecture table is not a component ablation.

The claim of preserving diagnostic accuracy is overstated: on MIMIC-CXR, the proposed method decreases accuracy from 85.46 to 84.26 and AUC from 63.85 to 62.10. More importantly, aggregate accuracy and AUC do not establish clinical safety; subgroup sensitivity, specificity, calibration, and worst-group performance are absent.

The GradCAM evidence is qualitative, based on few examples, and its asserted heatmap separation is neither quantified nor validated by clinicians. Attention-map overlap cannot establish causal removal of demographic information or that highlighted regions are medically relevant.

Reproducibility is poor: preprocessing, uncertain-label handling, augmentation, model architectures, mask constraints, training epochs, validation selection, and exact sample construction are missing, while code and environments are only promised after publication. The TCGA-LUAD description also emphasizes genomic and clinical data without clearly documenting how CT images and patient-level labels were selected.

The evaluation only treats binary gender and does not examine race, age, intersectional groups, nonbinary or missing demographic labels, or external-site generalization. The assumption that all S-to-Y influence is legitimate while all S-to-X-to-prediction influence is biased is clinically contestable and requires domain justification and sensitivity analysis. Given that the causal theory and proposed metric underpin the main novelty, these are consequential shortcomings rather than minor correctable presentation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: reducing demographic bias in medical-image classifiers without discarding clinically relevant correlations.
The intuition behind conditioning fairness on the true diagnosis is potentially useful, since demographic parity can be inappropriate when disease prevalence genuinely differs between groups.
The evaluation covers three medical datasets, reports predictive and fairness metrics, compares against two adversarial baselines, and includes architecture and hyperparameter studies.
The presentation is generally easy to follow, with clear overview diagrams and compact quantitative tables.
weaknesses: The central causal argument is technically unsound. The paper defines total causal effect using observational quantities P(Y-hat|S), rather than interventional distributions, and does not establish the assumptions needed to identify its proposed path-specific effect from observational data.

The proof of Theorem 1 contains invalid algebra: factors including P(Y-hat|X) and P(X|Y) disappear between Eqs. 13 and 14. Its necessity argument merely asserts that one condition is a special case of another, without supplying a counterexample or proving the claimed non-implication.

The interpretation of Theorem 2 is reversed in the subsequent text. The theorem claims that I(S;X|Y)=0 is sufficient for I(S;Y-hat|Y)=0, but the paper then states that the latter is sufficient for the former. Consequently, a low ADF does not establish the claimed Diagnosis Fairness: predictions may conceal sensitive information even when X still contains it, and output conditional independence does not validate the proposed causal path removal.

The optimization is not shown to implement the stated theory. The discriminator loss uses I(S-hat;S), not the conditional mutual information I(S;X|Y), and the manuscript does not explain how any mutual-information term or ADF is estimated. Conditioning a discriminator on Y alone does not establish that the learned perturbation performs a causal intervention or removes a particular causal path.

The structural causal model is asserted rather than justified. It assumes S causes the true diagnosis and image, while Y causes the image, but discusses no confounding, selection, measurement, label-generation, or identifiability assumptions. Intervening on gender is also conceptually delicate and requires a much more careful counterfactual interpretation.

The empirical evidence is insufficiently specified and internally inconsistent. Table 1 says all models use ResNet50, yet its MIMIC and CheXpert results exactly match the ResNet18 rows in Table 2. The selected main results also do not consistently match the appendix settings alpha=1 and beta=1 or the associated ablation rows.

Essential reproducibility details are absent: cohort and subgroup sizes after filtering, patient-level split procedure, validation/model-selection protocol, uncertainty-label handling, image and TCGA preprocessing, generator/discriminator architectures, perturbation bounds, MI estimators, thresholds, and baseline tuning. A single 90/10 split is reported with no independent test set, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

The evaluation does not report group-specific sensitivity, specificity, AUC, calibration, or worst-group performance, despite making clinical-equity claims. Aggregate accuracy is particularly uninformative here because chest-X-ray accuracy is around 85% while AUC is only 62–65%, suggesting substantial class imbalance or threshold effects.

Only two debiasing baselines are considered, with no comparison to stronger recent causal, conditional-adversarial, reweighting, or subgroup-robust approaches. It is unclear whether all methods receive comparable tuning and perturbation budgets.

The Grad-CAM examples are qualitative and apparently selected without a quantitative localization or overlap study. Spatial separation between diagnosis and sensitive-attribute heatmaps does not demonstrate causal disentanglement, medical relevance, or removal of demographic bias.

The broad claims of robustness, interpretability, and applicability to clinical decision support substantially exceed the evidence. Only binary gender is studied, important intersectional and external-site evaluations are absent, and there is no meaningful discussion of failure modes or clinical deployment risks. Given the invalid theoretical foundation and unreliable experimental account, the paper does not currently provide a convincing scientific case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, high-impact problem: reducing demographic bias in medical-image diagnosis without discarding clinically legitimate relationships between demographic attributes and disease.
The distinction between direct demographic influence and clinically mediated influence is intuitive and potentially more appropriate for medicine than enforcing unconditional demographic parity.
Reported results across MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, and TCGA-LUAD consistently improve ADF, demographic parity, and equal opportunity over the included baselines while retaining most predictive performance.
The paper evaluates several architectures and hyperparameters and supplements aggregate metrics with downstream-task and Grad-CAM analyses.

The presentation is compact and generally understandable, with a helpful causal diagram and a clear high-level account of the proposed adversarial masking framework. weaknesses: The central theoretical justification contains consequential errors. In Theorem 1, P(Y-hat|X) is improperly moved outside the summation and then disappears during the transition to Eq. 14; the claimed non-necessity also does not follow merely by calling Eq. 16 a special case. More seriously, after Theorem 2 proves that I(S;X|Y)=0 is sufficient but not necessary for I(S;Y-hat|Y)=0, the text reverses this implication and incorrectly states that ADF is sufficient for the representation-level condition. These problems undermine the claimed causal guarantees.

ADF is the observational conditional mutual information I(S;Y-hat|Y), closely related to the established equalized-odds conditional-independence criterion. The paper does not convincingly establish its novelty as a causal metric, nor engage adequately with counterfactual fairness, path-specific fairness, and causal-fairness literature. A low ADF alone does not identify or prove removal of a causal path.

The causal model and identifying assumptions are insufficiently defended for the medical settings. Path-specific effects require strong structural and cross-world assumptions, yet there is no discussion of unmeasured confounding, selection effects, measurement error, or whether the proposed edge interventions are identifiable from these observational datasets.

Experimental reporting has notable inconsistencies. Table 1 says all models use ResNet50, but its MIMIC and CheXpert results exactly match the ResNet18 rows in Table 2. Results under the stated default alpha and beta also do not align clearly with the main table. Dataset sizes after filtering, group counts, patient-level splitting, validation and threshold-selection procedures, uncertainty labels, repetitions, confidence intervals, and significance tests are absent.

ADF estimation is not specified sufficiently: it is unclear whether predictions are thresholded, how conditional mutual information is estimated, and how estimator bias or class/group imbalance is handled. Without uncertainty estimates, the small reported values and differences are difficult to interpret.

The empirical comparison is limited to two debiasing baselines, and the proposed metric directly matches the training objective, making broader evaluation especially important. There are no subgroup sensitivity/specificity or calibration results, no intersectional evaluation, no race or age experiments despite broader claims, and no external-site generalization study.

The data-utility experiment has no relevant baseline, so it cannot show that the MI objective improves transfer. Likewise, the Grad-CAM examples are qualitative, apparently unpaired across methods, and lack quantitative localization or expert validation; spatial separation from a sensitive-attribute heatmap does not establish clinical relevance or causal disentanglement.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: generator/discriminator architectures, mask bounds and norm, optimization schedule, preprocessing, label handling, and concrete implementations of the mutual-information losses are not fully provided. Code and environments are only promised after publication.

Given the medical application, the paper should discuss failure modes and deployment risks more carefully, including whether suppressing sex-linked anatomy can remove genuinely diagnostic evidence and how fairness-performance choices would be validated clinically. Assessed as Algorithms/General because no contribution type is declared; under that category, the theoretical errors and insufficiently controlled evidence outweigh the promising empirical direction.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: mitigating demographic bias in high-dimensional medical images while attempting to preserve clinically relevant pathways.
Replacing explicit high-dimensional counterfactual density estimation with a discriminative conditional-independence objective is an appealing and potentially scalable direction.

The evaluation spans three datasets, multiple architectures, two sensitive-attribute definitions, several baselines, five-run uncertainty estimates, hyperparameter analyses, computational-cost reporting, and a synthetic experiment.
The reported results consistently show substantial improvements in observational fairness metrics with relatively modest losses in accuracy and AUC.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not established as stated. Theorem 1 is presented for arbitrary random variables, but its proof introduces unstated ignorability, consistency, causal-graph, and mediation assumptions. In particular, it replaces an edge intervention with an observational conditional distribution via P(X|Y,do(S))=P(X|Y,S). This identification does not follow from conditional independence alone and is especially delicate because Y is a descendant of S. The theorem must be reformulated under explicit structural assumptions and justified using valid edge-intervention identification.

The paper conflates observational conditional independence with path-specific counterfactual fairness. Low I(S;Y-hat|Y) follows from the proposed representation condition under a Markov assumption, but the converse does not hold. Consequently, the reported Equalized Odds values cannot verify that I(S;X|Y)=0 or that the path-specific direct effect has been removed, contrary to repeated claims of observability and empirical validation.

The implemented adversarial objective is insufficiently derived. The discriminator receives Y and predicts S, yet Y may legitimately contain information about S. Simply reducing I(S-hat;S) or increasing prediction entropy is not shown to minimize the conditional mutual information I(S;X-tilde|Y); it can instead oppose the very S-to-Y relationship the method claims to preserve. The estimators for I(S-hat;S), H(S-hat), and I(Y-hat;Y), and their relation to the stated min-max problem, are not specified.

The data-utility argument is unconvincing. Maximizing I(X-tilde;E) does not specifically preserve information traveling along S-to-Y-to-X and may preserve sensitive information as well. No theorem connects this generic input-reconstruction-style objective to preservation of the fair indirect effect.

The method is not reproducible from the manuscript. The generator and discriminator architectures, mask bounds and iterative procedure, mutual-information estimators used in the actual losses, optimization schedule, image preprocessing, label handling, dataset sample counts, and whether medical-image splits are patient-level are omitted. Patient-level splitting is essential for MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert because image-level splitting can cause leakage. The advertised code link is blank, while the appendix only promises release after publication.

The synthetic validation omits essential information, including the prediction mechanism Y-hat, training procedure, sample size, and causal-effect estimator. Equation 25 alone is therefore insufficient to reproduce the reported direct and indirect effects or establish that SPARC preserves the intended pathway.

Several ablation results are internally inconsistent with the main configuration. Although the paper states eta=0.2, alpha=1, and beta=1, the corresponding rows in Tables 4-6 give materially different results from one another and from Table 1. The claimed monotonic performance decrease with increasing alpha is also contradicted by Table 5. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the experimental record and parameter-selection protocol.

The main experiments compare only observational fairness metrics and largely non-causal baselines. They do not measure conditional dependence at the masked input, discriminator optimality, mask magnitude or perceptual validity, subgroup calibration, worst-group clinical performance, or external-dataset generalization. Thus they cannot distinguish genuine path-specific mitigation from ordinary accuracy-fairness regularization or distribution-specific perturbation.

The Grad-CAM examples are qualitative and selectively presented; visual separation between two heatmaps is neither quantified nor evidence of causal disentanglement. Claims that predictions become medically relevant and that the direct causal effect is pruned are therefore unsupported.

No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. Under that standard, the potentially valuable idea and promising numerical results do not compensate for the unsupported causal identification, mismatch between theory and optimization, and insufficiently specified experimental protocol. These are consequential issues affecting the paper's principal scientific claim rather than minor correctable presentation problems.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important computer-vision problem: mitigating demographic bias in high-dimensional medical images while retaining clinically relevant information. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/8321c9d4921542d5a81d627cf2a557f3/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The proposed conditional adversary is computationally practical, with a reported 12% FLOP overhead, and can be applied to different backbones.

Experiments cover three datasets, two protected attributes, several architectures, five comparison methods, and five-run uncertainty estimates. The appendix adds validation-based tuning and a synthetic SCM experiment.
The authors explicitly acknowledge that conditional independence is sufficient but not necessary for their fairness target and may remove admissible sensitive-attribute information.
weaknesses: The central causal theorem is not established under the presented SCM. The proof replaces P(X|Y,do(S)) with P(X|Y,S) using an asserted 'ignorability and consistency' step, but the required identification assumptions are neither stated nor justified. Conditioning on Y, a descendant of S, and the depicted exogenous interaction between Y and X make this substitution especially problematic. Observational conditional independence S ⟂ X | Y does not generally identify the nested, path-specific intervention used to define the direct effect.

The method operationalizes an observational equalized-odds-style constraint rather than convincingly enforcing path-specific counterfactual fairness. Failure of a finite discriminator to predict S from the perturbed input given Y does not establish I(S;X|Y)=0, and minimizing mutual information between S and the discriminator output is not equivalent to minimizing mutual information between S and the input representation. No discriminator-capacity or sensitive-information leakage evaluation is supplied.

The paper conflates the original X appearing in the theorem and causal graph with the generated, masked input X-tilde used by the algorithm. It does not derive how altering an observed medical image through a learned perturbation corresponds to a valid intervention on the S→X path while holding the S→Y→X pathway fixed.

The experiments do not substantiate the claimed superior accuracy–fairness trade-off. Each method is shown at only one operating point, without Pareto curves or fairness-matched comparisons. SPARC generally reduces accuracy relative to Vanilla, and Appendix Table 9 incorrectly states that it outperforms Vanilla on both validation and test sets even though its reported accuracy is lower on every dataset.

Causal evidence is very limited. The only experiment that directly measures path-specific effects uses a simple one-dimensional synthetic SCM and compares only against Vanilla and AD. Established path-specific counterfactual-fairness methods are not evaluated, even in the low-dimensional setting where the manuscript acknowledges they are applicable.

The evaluation never directly reports the quantity optimized by the claimed reduction, I(S;X-tilde|Y), nor sensitive-attribute prediction accuracy under strong held-out attackers. Improvements in EOd computed from final predictions can arise without sensitive information being removed and therefore do not validate Theorem 1 or the asserted causal mechanism.

Important implementation details are absent, including generator and discriminator architectures, precise mask constraints and iterative procedure, optimization schedules, batch sizes, preprocessing, uncertainty-label handling, patient-level split protocol, MI estimation for the reported EOd, and the hyperparameter-selection objective. The advertised code link is blank, while the appendix says code will only be provided after publication, making the results presently difficult to reproduce.

The medical-image perturbations are not evaluated for realism, pathology preservation, robustness to alternative predictors, or clinical safety. Grad-CAM overlap is qualitative and cannot demonstrate causal disentanglement; assertions such as breast-region attention representing bias are speculative without expert annotation or quantitative localization analysis.

Dataset reporting is unclear. TCGA-LUAD is described primarily in terms of genomic profiles, whereas the method and Grad-CAM analysis appear to use images; the exact modality, cohort construction, sample counts, missing-data filtering, and possible patient leakage are not documented.

Because the default Algorithms/General contribution type applies, both the algorithmic mechanism and its causal justification require convincing validation. The potentially useful idea and broad benchmark coverage do not offset the consequential identification flaw and insufficient evidence for the paper's principal path-specific counterfactual-fairness claim.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: mitigating demographic bias in high-dimensional medical inputs while retaining clinically legitimate information. Treating the submission as Algorithms/General, the proposed conditional-adversarial masking framework is relevant and potentially useful.

The central reduction from difficult counterfactual estimation to a conditional-independence objective is intuitive and practically appealing. The paper also explicitly acknowledges that I(S;X|Y)=0 is sufficient but not necessary for path-specific counterfactual fairness and explains the possible over-constraint.

The evaluation spans three datasets, multiple architectures, gender and age attributes, five-run reporting, hyperparameter studies, computational overhead, and downstream-task utility. SPARC consistently improves the reported fairness metrics with comparatively modest losses in accuracy/AUC; for example, CheXpert EOd decreases from 11.18×10^-3 to 1.20×10^-3 while AUC changes from 65.93% to 64.99%.

The synthetic SCM experiment is valuable because it directly evaluates path-specific effects: SPARC reduces |DE| from 0.284 to 0.027 while retaining |IE|=0.171, whereas adversarial debiasing retains only 0.061. This supports the intended distinction better than observational fairness metrics alone.

The manuscript is generally well organized, includes a limitations-oriented discussion of the stricter sufficient condition, reports a validation-based hyperparameter experiment, and estimates a moderate 12% computational overhead.
weaknesses: The principal theorem is stated too generally. Observational I(S;X|Y)=0 does not by itself imply zero path-specific causal effect for arbitrary random variables. The proof additionally assumes consistency, ignorability, the particular SCM/edge intervention, and P(X|Y,do(S|πd))=P(X|Y,S), but these identifying assumptions are neither included in the theorem statement nor adequately justified. This is especially concerning because the causal diagram mentions unobserved exogenous interactions.

The optimized quantity is not shown to equal the theorem's condition. Training merely makes a finite discriminator's prediction Ŝ uninformative about S; this does not establish I(S;X̃|Y)=0 unless the discriminator is optimal and sufficiently expressive. No post-hoc sensitive-attribute leakage test, discriminator convergence evidence, or estimate/bound on conditional MI is provided. Likewise, low EOd cannot validate Theorem 1 or PSCF because the theorem is only one-way and EOd concerns predictions rather than the path-specific causal effect.

The claim that MI pretraining preserves the legitimate indirect path is under-supported. Maximizing I(X̃;E) preserves general input information, not specifically S→Y→X→Ŷ information, and there is no theorem connecting this objective to preservation of the indirect effect. Direct causal effects are tested only in a simple one-dimensional synthetic SCM, so the central causal claim remains weakly established for the real datasets.

Important experimental and reproducibility details are missing. The paper does not say whether chest-radiograph splits are patient-disjoint, which is essential because these datasets contain multiple studies per patient. TCGA-LUAD is described in terms of genomic and clinical data but processed with ResNet50 and visualized using GradCAM on apparent images; the exact imaging modality, cohort size, preprocessing, and sampling unit are unclear. The manuscript also contains a blank code link and later says code will be released only after publication.

The hyperparameter ablations are internally inconsistent with the claimed final configuration. The text states η=0.2, α=1, and β=1, yet the corresponding rows in Tables 4–6 do not reproduce the main results and differ substantially from one another. Table 5 also claims performance gradually decreases with α although the reported values do not show that pattern. These discrepancies make it difficult to determine the actual training protocol or whether comparisons were controlled.

The medical evaluation relies primarily on overall accuracy/AUC and very small aggregate fairness gaps. It lacks subgroup sample counts and subgroup-specific sensitivity, specificity, calibration, or uncertainty intervals, as well as statistical tests for method-to-method differences. Random in-distribution splits across related medical datasets are also insufficient to support broad claims about deployment or generalization.

The GradCAM analysis is qualitative and its assertion that reduced heatmap overlap demonstrates removal of the direct causal path is not warranted. Attention localization is neither a causal explanation nor a quantitative measure of disentanglement. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but the theorem-to-objective gap and reporting inconsistencies slightly outweigh the positive empirical evidence in the current version.
